item.title: Falcon Heavy set to launch classified NROL-97 to high-energy orbit
item.dc:creator: Eleanor Day
item.description:
SpaceX’s Falcon Heavy is poised atop Launch Complex 39A once again, this time to launch…

The post Falcon Heavy set to launch classified NROL-97 to high-energy orbit appeared first on NASASpaceFlight.com.
item.content:encoded:
SpaceX’s Falcon Heavy is poised atop Launch Complex 39A once again, this time to launch the classified NROL-97 payload for the United States National Reconnaissance Office. Falcon Heavy is scheduled to liftoff from the Kennedy Space Center at 11:53 PM EDT (03:53 UTC) on Oct. 1, following a trajectory into a high-energy orbit.

The mission will mark the quickest turnaround between Falcon Heavy missions, with the rocket having last launched the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope for NASA on Aug. 30. As with that mission, the two side boosters will be recovered, while the center core will be expended.

Falcon Heavy and launch details

Falcon Heavy is expected to launch from Launch Complex 39A (LC-39A) at the Kennedy Space Center (KSC) in Florida on Thursday, Oct. 1. A 59-minute launch window opens at 11:53 PM EDT (03:53 UTC), running until 12:52 AM EDT (04:52 UTC) on Oct. 2. In the event of a scrub, a backup opportunity is available for the following day at 11:48 PM EDT.

See Also

  • NROL-97 Updates
  • SpaceX Forum Section
  • NSF Store
  • Click here to Join L2

The vehicle will launch on a northeasterly trajectory to deliver a classified payload for the National Reconnaissance Office (NRO) to a high-energy orbit. Due to the payload’s mass, Falcon Heavy’s center core, booster B1106, will be expended to maximize stage performance and ensure the classified payload is placed on the correct trajectory. B1106 will be on its first and final flight, a common practice for Falcon Heavy center cores.

The outer boosters, B1072 and B1104, will land at Landing Zones 2 (LZ-2) and 1 (LZ-1), respectively. B1072 will be on its fourth flight, previously supporting the GOES-U, ViaSat 3 F3, and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope missions. B1104 will be on its second flight, having previously supported the Nancy Grace Roman Telescope mission as well.

Falcon Heavy is SpaceX’s super-heavy-lift, partially reusable launch vehicle that can deliver up to 63,800 kg to low-Earth orbit and 26,700 kg to geostationary transfer orbit. The 70-m-tall vehicle has 5.2-m-diameter fairing halves. The first stage features three side-by-side Falcon boosters, each powered by nine Merlin 1D sea-level engines fueled by kerosene (RP-1) and liquid oxygen (LOX). The outer boosters are usually recovered on land via return-to-launch-site (RTLS) trajectories, with the center core mostly expended.

Falcon Heavy and its 27 Merlin engines in the hangar at Launch Complex 39A in Florida pic.twitter.com/ETejT6zPD2

— SpaceX (@SpaceX) September 28, 2026

The second stage uses a single Merlin 1D vacuum-optimized engine, capable of multiple restarts, and is fueled by RP-1 and LOX. Unlike the first stage boosters, the second stage is expended. In total, Falcon Heavy has a total liftoff thrust of 22,819 kilonewtons (kN).

The NROL-97 payload

As usual for a National Reconnaissance Office (NRO) mission, the exact identity and technical details of the NROL-97 payload are classified. However, opting for Falcon Heavy — particularly a configuration that uses an expended center core –suggests a high-mass payload. The targeted “high-energy orbit” also points to potential orbital destinations such as the geostationary-Earth orbit (GEO), medium-Earth orbit (MEO), or a highly elliptical orbit (HEO).

Unlike low-Earth orbit (LEO) reconnaissance assets that offer brief imaging windows, payloads in high-energy orbits can provide continuous coverage of specific regions. These orbits are frequently used for intelligence, missile-warning, or missile-defense satellites, as well as Earth observation and weather satellites. The NRO likely will not disclose any payload details in the near future.

Following NROL-97, Falcon Heavy’s next mission, Griffin Mission One, is scheduled to launch no earlier than December 2026. The mission will see Falcon Heavy launch an Astrobotic-developed lunar lander under NASA’s Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) program. The vehicle will perform a trans-lunar injection burn to deliver the uncrewed 6,360 kg Griffin One lander to the lunar surface.

Falcon Heavy rolls out to LC-39A with NROL-97. (Credit: SpaceX)

The next mission after this, Astrobotic Lunar Mission 3, is tentatively scheduled for 2027. The commercial flight will deliver payloads to the Moon’s South Pole aboard another Astrobotic lander; these potentially include the FLEX Lunar Innovation Platform (FLIP) rover developed by Venturi Astrolab. Alongside its lunar missions, Falcon Heavy is scheduled to launch a heavy payload manifest for the United States Space Force (USSF) and the National Reconnaissance Office (NRO) in 2027.

Despite the Falcon family’s pending retirement in the coming years, Falcon Heavy’s manifest is full, and it will likely continue flying for several years until Starship becomes fully operational and can take over SpaceX’s heavy-lift missions.

(Lead Image: The NROL-97 Falcon Heavy sits atop LC-39A. Credit: SpaceX)

The post Falcon Heavy set to launch classified NROL-97 to high-energy orbit appeared first on NASASpaceFlight.com.

item.title: Canada Rocket Company plans first large-scale engine test site in London, Ontario
item.dc:creator: Chris Bergin
item.description:
Canada Rocket Company (CRC) will build Canada’s first large-scale rocket engine test facility at London…

The post Canada Rocket Company plans first large-scale engine test site in London, Ontario appeared first on NASASpaceFlight.com.
item.content:encoded:
Canada Rocket Company (CRC) will build Canada’s first large-scale rocket engine test facility at London International Airport, a $30 million complex intended for static firing of the company’s methalox engines as it develops a reusable medium-lift launch vehicle.

The Jeremy Hansen Test Facility is named for Canadian astronaut Jeremy Hansen, the first Canadian to fly around the Moon.

CRC will lease 50 acres from the Greater London International Airport Authority for an engine test area and a 12,000-square-foot office and shop building used for engineering, assembly, and test preparation.

Putting the shop next to the stands is meant to keep engine build-up, instrumentation, and test ops in one place rather than splitting that work across distant sites.
The test area is planned for up to three vertical and horizontal stands, with the ability to static-fire engines producing more than 1 MN of thrust. Vertical stands are typically used for flight-like firings. Horizontal stands are often used earlier in a campaign for access, instrumentation, and engine development work.

CRC said the site is a foundational step toward sovereign Canadian launch capability. The company expects the facility to be fully operational by 2028 and said it is working with the airport, regulators, and the local community as planning advances.

CRC is developing a reusable medium-lift rocket capable of delivering up to 12,500 kg to sun-synchronous orbit, powered by its own E-1 methalox engine.

The company, founded in 2025, says it is backed by a team that includes SpaceX and Blue Origin alumni and cites more than 150 years of combined orbital launch experience.

“Canada’s path to its own access to space starts on the ground. This facility is where our engineering becomes hardware, and where we put our engines to the test,” said Hugh Kolias, CEO and co-founder of Canada Rocket Company.

“Building in London means investing in Canadian talent and giving our team the tools to turn rocket designs into proven technology. We look forward to working with the London community to build that capability here.”
CRC expects to create about 40 skilled jobs at the London site in the next 18 months, covering engineering, fabrication, and test preparation. The broader vehicle program is projected to generate roughly 1,000 jobs and more than $1 billion in additional investment over the next decade.

The company is also forming training and workforce partnerships with Western University and Fanshawe College to grow the regional aerospace talent pipeline.

London Economic Development Corporation president and CEO Kapil Lakhotia said the project adds a new dimension to a city that already hosts more than 40 defence and aerospace companies.

“With more than 40 defence and aerospace companies already operating here, London has the expertise, talent and ecosystem to support this kind of innovation,” he said. “We’re thrilled to welcome Canada Rocket Company to London and support what comes next.”
CRC argues that medium-lift remains the class most missions need, even as the largest providers shift toward heavy-lift vehicles and capacity reserved for their own constellations.

The London stands will not put a rocket into orbit, but they are the ground infrastructure CRC needs before an engine like E-1 can be treated as flight hardware.

Renders via Canada Rocket Co (CRC).

item.title: Starfish Otter, other payloads launch on Transporter 18
item.dc:creator: Justin Davenport
item.description:
SpaceX launched a Transporter rideshare mission aboard a Falcon 9 from California, on the same…

The post Starfish Otter, other payloads launch on Transporter 18 appeared first on NASASpaceFlight.com.
item.content:encoded:
SpaceX launched a Transporter rideshare mission aboard a Falcon 9 from California, on the same day as the Crew-13 and NROL-97 Falcon Heavy missions were scheduled out of Florida. This is the first time in a while that the company is using all three Falcon-capable launch pads in the same general time period.

Transporter 18 flew on Thursday, Oct. 1 at 11:32 AM PDT (18:32 UTC) from Space Launch Complex 4E (SLC-4E) at Vandenberg Space Force Base. The 58-minute launch window ended at 12:16 PM PDT (19:16 UTC), and this was the 110th Falcon 9 mission of 2026. The mission’s 130 payloads featured a prototype AI satellite for Google, the NASA-funded SPRITE telescope, and Starfish’s first Otter servicing vehicle, among others.

The rocket took a southerly trajectory suitable for sun-synchronous orbiting payloads. Following stage separation, the first stage, B1082-25, conducted a return-to-launch-site maneuver before safely touching down at Landing Zone 4 near its launch pad. The booster started its career with the Starlink 7-9 mission and launched on 20 additional Starlink flights, as well as the USSF-62, OneWeb #20, and NROL-145 missions.

Artist’s impression of the SPRITE satellite in orbit. (Credit: University of Colorado/LASP)

After the second stage finished the second burn of its Merlin Vac engine at T+51:07, the mission’s payloads were released during an 11-minute period from T+54:22 to T+1:05:15. NASA’s SPRITE payload started off the deployment sequence, and the separation of Varda Space’s W-8 space factory marked the final release.

Google’s Project Suncatcher M1 prototype, which deployed at T+1:01:25, is an experimental satellite to test data processing hardware in orbit for future space-based AI data centers. The satellite will evaluate how Google’s Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) handle launch vibrations and space radiation, as well as approaches to cooling the chips.

Data centers in space could become the next major application to use low-Earth orbit, with constellations like SpaceX’s Starmind, designed to launch on Starship, already planned. Google’s prototype is among the first of its kind, and the company plans to test a laser link between two of its Suncatcher prototypes in 2027.

BREAKING: Google $GOOGL will launch an experimental AI satellite on Oct. 1 carrying four of its TPU chips, the New York Times reports, marking the first orbital test for Project Suncatcher – Google’s effort to eventually build AI data centers in space.

The satellite will test… pic.twitter.com/yaDbC8VzaH

— Outer Space Today (@outerspacetoday) September 24, 2026

Another notable payload on Transporter 18 was Starfish Space’s Otter satellite servicing vehicle. Otter, which was released at T+1:03:06, is a 335 kg satellite contracted by NASA to autonomously inspect multiple dead US-owned satellites in orbit. The mission, known as Small Spacecraft Propulsion and Inspection Capability or SSPICY, will last up to two years.

During the SSPICY mission, Otter will gather spin rate, spin-axis, and surface condition data on satellites after approaching them within hundreds of meters. SSPICY is a precursor to future life extension and satellite deorbiting mission, for which Starfish Space has contracts from Intelsat and the US military.

NASA sponsored other payloads on Transporter 18. One of them was the very first payload to be released, SPRITE, at T+54:22. SPRITE, also known as the Supernova Remnants and Proxies for Reionization Testbed Experiment, is a 12U CubeSat that will study shock waves in supernova remnants and ionizing radiation from low-redshift star-forming galaxies.

Artist’s impression of the Exolaunch deployer releasing satellites. (Credit: Exolaunch)

Another NASA payload is GPDM, or Green Propulsion Dual Mode. GPDM, which was deployed at T+55:34, will test a low-toxicity “green” propellant for a dual-mode system that can support high-impulse and high-efficiency spacecraft maneuvers.

See Also

  • Transporter-18 Updates
  • SpaceX Missions Section
  • L2 SpaceX Section
  • Click here to Join L2

Varda Space manifested the W-8 and W-9 satellites as the final payloads set for deployment, starting with W-9 at T+1:04:56. These satellites host small factories that can make pharmaceuticals or other materials, which then transfer into a reentry capsule that touches down safely back on Earth.

Spacecraft separation systems provider Exolaunch deployed 45 satellites on this mission as part of its rideshare program. Among these payloads are four spacecraft for Finnish intelligence company ICEYE, which operates a constellation of Earth-observation satellites.

Additionally, D-Orbit, Planet Labs, OHB Italia, Satellogic, SEOPS, and other entities also had payloads booked on Transporter 18.  Moreover, a number of countries, government agencies, and private corporations were represented in the payload manifest.

ICEYE-2 is one of the payloads scheduled to fly on Transporter 18. (Credit: SpaceX)

Rideshare missions like this one have been used to build up constellations like ICEYE, offer countries the ability to launch their first satellite, and to fly experiments that might not have been feasible to fund and fly before. However, these missions may not continue past 2028 as SpaceX gradually winds down Falcon 9 operations in favor of Starship.

Three more Transporter missions, numbered 19, 20, and 21, remain on the Falcon 9 manifest, with Transporter 19 scheduled for launch no earlier (NET) than February 2027. Next, Transporter 20 is to fly NET June, and Transporter 21 will launch NET October 2027. The launch site for these future Transporter missions is not known yet, as these missions to sun-synchronous orbit can fly from either the West Coast or Florida.

A previous Varda Space satellite seen during processing. (Credit: Rocket Lab)

SpaceX is also winding down its Bandwagon series, a similar rideshare that flies payloads to a mid-latitude orbit with three launches left, all from Florida. The current schedule has Bandwagon-5 for sometime in October, while listing Bandwagon-6 as NET 2027, and Bandwagon-7 set to fly in the first quarter of 2028. That flight will likely be the last ever rideshare mission a Falcon 9 flies, as Starship takes up more of SpaceX’s manifest.

(Lead image: Screenshot of Transporter 18 launching from SLC-4E in California on Oct. 1, 2026. Credit: SpaceX)

The post Starfish Otter, other payloads launch on Transporter 18 appeared first on NASASpaceFlight.com.

item.title: Crew-13 astronauts launch to ISS after weeks of delays
item.dc:creator: Sawyer Rosenstein
item.description:
One veteran astronaut and three first-time flyers began a six-month mission to the International Space…

The post Crew-13 astronauts launch to ISS after weeks of delays appeared first on NASASpaceFlight.com.
item.content:encoded:
One veteran astronaut and three first-time flyers began a six-month mission to the International Space Station as part of the NASA and SpaceX Crew-13 mission. NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney, as well as Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk and cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov, launched on Thursday, Oct. 1, aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. This mission is also set to mark the shortest time between launch and docking for any Crew Dragon vehicle.

Crew Dragon C213, named Grace, flew on its second-ever mission and its first long-duration stay at the orbiting laboratory. It first flew in June 2025 as part of the Axiom-4 mission and spent just over 20 days in space.

With the on-time launch at 11:10 AM EDT (15:10 UTC) on Oct. 1, the crew will spend only about eight hours and 50 minutes free-flying before their capsule autonomously docks with the forward port of the Station’s Harmony module. The previous record was set by Crew-11, which made the journey in just under 15 hours.

Issues with the capsule pushed the launch from a Sept. 12 attempt to its current date. According to NASA, during standard prelaunch spacecraft processing, an oxidizer leak was found in Dragon’s propulsion system. The Crew Dragon vehicle is equipped with 16 Draco thrusters for on-orbit maneuvering. It utilizes hypergolic propellants, meaning they ignite upon contact with each other. SpaceX uses monomethyl hydrazine as fuel and nitrogen tetroxide as oxidizer.

See Also

  • Crew-13 Updates
  • ISS Forum Section
  • NSF Store
  • Click here to Join L2

The crew of four waited patiently in Houston while the problem was solved and arrived in Florida on Sept. 26 ahead of the launch. They also participated in a dry dress rehearsal on Sept. 29, which involved running through all the launch-day activities up to liftoff with no propellants loaded into the rocket.

Crew-13’s commander, NASA astronaut Jessica Watkins, is the only spaceflight veteran of this crew. She joined NASA as part of the 2017 astronaut class and first flew aboard Crew Dragon Freedom on its inaugural flight, Crew-4. This would also make her the first active NASA astronaut to fly twice on Crew Dragon and the fourth person ever to do so, joining Axiom astronauts Peggy Whitson and Michael López-Alegria, cosmonaut Andrew Fedyaev, and now-NASA administrator Jared Isaacman.

She spent 170 days in space supporting Expeditions 67 and 68, conducting extensive science and research, which she is very familiar with. Prior to her selection as an astronaut, Watkins was a postdoctoral fellow at the California Institute of Technology, following her studies at UCLA in planetary science and geology. She was a member of the science team for the Curiosity Mars rover. At NASA, she also became an aquanaut as part of the NEEMO underwater research program.

Crew-13 arrives at the Kennedy Space Center ahead of launch. From left to right: Teteryatnikov, Delaney, Watkins, and Kutryk. (Credit: Julia Bergeron for NSF)

Crew-13’s pilot is the Florida-born and raised NASA astronaut Luke Delaney. Delaney was first selected to be a NASA astronaut in 2021 as part of the 23rd astronaut class.

Luke enlisted with the U.S. Marine Corps in 1998 as a naval aviator. He saw combat in December 2001 in Afghanistan as part of Operation Enduring Freedom. After returning and primarily flying the KC-130, he eventually became a test pilot instructor on the T-6B, C-12C, U-6A, and NU-1B aircraft. In total, including time with NASA, Delaney has logged more than 3,700 hours of flight time in 48 different aircraft. After leaving the Marines in 2020, he joined NASA’s Langley Research Center in Virginia to assist with airborne science missions.

“A lot of what we’re doing on Earth to better understand space, we’re doing in space to better understand Earth,” Delaney said in an August 2026 interview with NSF.

Crew-13 mission specialist Joshua Kutryk, set to be the first Canadian astronaut to fly as part of NASA’s Commercial Crew Program, is preparing for his first trip to space. He will be the second Canadian to fly on a Crew Dragon capsule following Mark Pathy’s flight as part of the first Axiom private mission. Kutryk was one of two people selected for the Canadian Space Agency’s (CSA) 2017 astronaut group, alongside Jenni Gibbons. The latter became part of the Artemis II backup crew and was a CAPCOM during the historic lunar flyby mission.

Watkins, Kutryk, and Delaney during EVA suit training ahead of launch. (Credit: NASA)

While this is his first flight into space, this is not the first flight he has been assigned to. In 2023, it was announced Kutryk would fly as part of the first operational crew flight of Boeing’s Starliner vehicle. However, following the Crew Flight Test with Butch Wilmore and Suni Williams — which would later be classified as a Type A mishap, the most severe at NASA — Starliner-1 was switched to a cargo resupply mission.

Of the four astronauts scheduled to fly on Starliner at the time of the mission’s reassignment, Mike Fincke and Kimia Yui would go on to fly aboard Crew-11, while its planned commander Scott Tingle now heads the astronaut office at NASA. This left Kutryk in limbo until April 2026, when he was selected for Crew-13.

Born in Alberta, he would go on to graduate from the Royal Military College of Canada before getting master’s degrees at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University and Air University in the US and again at the Royal Military College of Canada. He graduated from test pilot school at Edwards Air Force Base and flew with the Royal Canadian Air Force flying the CF-188. He saw deployments to Afghanistan and Libya.

The second mission specialist, Russian cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatrikov, was selected by Roscosmos in Jan. 2021. He graduated from Russia’s Naval Engineering Institute before going on to work on submarines.

Crew Dragon Grace arrives at SLC-40 in late September for integration with Falcon 9. (Credit: SpaceX)

Crew-13 launched from SpaceX’s Space Launch Complex 40 (SLC-40) at the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. SpaceX removed the crew access arm at historic Launch Complex 39A (LC-39A) several months ago, meaning all future crew missions are expected to launch from SLC-40.

The booster that carried them to space was B1101, flying on its third mission. It first flew a Starlink mission in January 2026, then launched Crew-12 in February. That crew is set to return back to Earth shortly after Crew-13’s arrival. The booster for this mission will likely fly again after this mission, as it performed a return-to-launch-site (RTLS) landing at Landing Zone 40 (LZ-40), located directly adjacent to SLC-40.

This mission comes at an interesting time. SpaceX’s President and COO Gwynne Shotwell, when asked about Crew Dragon’s future, said it is not being retired today but indicated a slowdown in the program and noted Starliner’s lack of flights to the Station. So far in September, NASA has announced that Crew-15, Crew-16, and Crew-17 will all fly aboard a Crew Dragon in addition to the already assigned Crew-14.

At a NASA media briefing prior to the Crew-13 launch, officials said they plan to fly astronauts aboard Starliner by 2028 and acknowledged their interest in exercising their option for a fifth and sixth flight to the Station with the Boeing capsule.

(Lead image: Falcon 9 and Crew Dragon Grace launch from SLC-40 on Crew-13. Credit: Julia Bergeron for NSF)

The post Crew-13 astronauts launch to ISS after weeks of delays appeared first on NASASpaceFlight.com.

item.title: Starship makes orbit, Flight 15 preps in full swing
item.dc:creator: Ryan Weber
item.description:
SpaceX made significant strides in the Starship program during Flight 14. Booster 21, despite losing…

The post Starship makes orbit, Flight 15 preps in full swing appeared first on NASASpaceFlight.com.
item.content:encoded:
SpaceX made significant strides in the Starship program during Flight 14. Booster 21, despite losing a few engines, still completed its entire flight. Ship 41 reached orbit despite losing a Raptor Vacuum engine on ascent, deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites, and returned safely to the Pacific Ocean just north of Hawaii.

While a post-flight review will take place internally, SpaceX is already staging for the next flight and a potential return to catching vehicles, with Flight 15 possibly taking place in October.

Flight 14 Review:

The prelaunch chilldown for this launch resembled the Wet Dress Rehearsal (WDR) conducted on Sept. 24, in which the methane reclaim vent started up one hour 30 minutes before propellant load instead of two hours, compared to Flights 12 and 13. This will make tank farm operations with a full stack quicker in the future.

This was already after SpaceX had pushed the launch by 31 minutes; SpaceX would end up pushing the launch to 7:48:59 am CDT after a quick hold at T-00:56:47. Later in the flight, SpaceX said the delays were to ensure better lighting at their Pacific Ocean splashdown points.

LAUNCH! Starship Flight 14 launches from Starbase Pad 2 on its first orbital mission attempt.

Live on X and YT:https://t.co/qFSXNsNURa pic.twitter.com/YcZoz3Rndr

— NSF – NASASpaceflight.com (@NASASpaceflight) September 28, 2026

The rest of the countdown proceeded without any holds or issues, as Booster 21 and Ship 41 were filled with around 5,500 metric tons of propellant and then went straight to liftoff. Liftoff was right at 7:48:59 am CDT, and Booster 21 had all 33 engines running right at liftoff.

Then, at T+ 00:01:16, a single Raptor engine in the inner ring of 10 went out; however, Booster 21 continued to hot staging with 32 of 33 engines.

At hot staging, Ship 41 ignited all six Raptor engines, and Booster 21 ignited 31 of 33 for the initial phase of the boost back burn. The engine that was turned off during ascent still appeared to glow as the booster aft section appeared on the ship flap cam. Booster 21 completed its full-duration boost back burn, going from 31 Raptors to 11, then down to 3 before shutting down and starting the glide back. 

Starship’s Raptor engines ignite during hot-staging separation. Super Heavy boosted back towards its splashdown site in the Gulf of America pic.twitter.com/0DcBz1wayt

— SpaceX (@SpaceX) September 28, 2026

See Also

  • SpaceX Starship Program
  • L2 SpaceX Section
  • NSF Store
  • Click here to Join L2

Booster 21 then completed its glide back and lit only 11 of 13 engines for the landing burn; the two engines that did not light were the same ones lost on ascent and during boost-back startup.

Booster 21 then completed its landing burn by performing a soft splashdown in the Gulf before blowing up. SpaceX intentionally set off the Flight Termination System as a “test of the safety system”, but also to turn the booster into thousands of pieces, so they wouldn’t have to go salvage anything.

Booster 21 also used a different landing profile than the previous several boosters that have actually landed.

In footage captured by NSF photographers as it came through the clouds, the booster uses its initial 13-engine burn to bleed off tons of speed, then switches down to five engines.

Once down to five engines, the booster pitches toward the tower to get close, then levels out while gimbaling the ignited engines to roll into the proper orientation to be caught by Pad 2’s chopsticks.

Booster 21 lands! pic.twitter.com/1PgY1R6LPC

— NSF – NASASpaceflight.com (@NASASpaceflight) September 28, 2026

The maneuver is required because Pad 2’s tower faces southeast and differs from all the other towers SpaceX is currently building. It was built this way because of land constraints when the pad was being built.

Ship 41’s ascent went well until T+ 00:07:18, when Engine 6 Raptor Vacuum SN 127 shut down. This marks the second time in three Block 3 flights that a Raptor Vacuum engine has gone out during the ascent burn. Luckily, though, Block 3 has engine-out capability, and Ship 41 made it to second-stage engine cutoff at T+00:08:35 by burning a little longer. 

Then came the nerve-racking wait to hear whether or not this issue with the Raptor Vacuum would make SpaceX abort the orbital injection burn. Without the burn, Ship 41 was on a suborbital track of -40 x 278 km at a 30.5-degree inclination, which is a bit off the 32 degrees they are authorized for Starlink V3.

Go for orbit! Starship will soon perform a burn with a single Raptor engine to enter an ~275 km orbit of Earth pic.twitter.com/HQxgQYc4eZ

— SpaceX (@SpaceX) September 28, 2026

At T+00:11:20, Dan Huot, SpaceX’s Communications Manager, announced that launch control had decided not to go for orbit because of Raptor vacuum issues encountered during ascent. Then, about a minute later, Dan Huot announced that teams were still reviewing the data and might change their mind about trying for orbit. 

After a near-10-min wait, SpaceX mission control polled: Go for orbit!

Next up came the orbital insertion burn, which started at T+ 00:25:20 and was a 95 m/s burn that placed Ship 41 in a 262 by 275 km, 30.5-degree inclination orbit. Then, after a short coast, the first of 26 Starlinks left the payload bay at T+ 00:35:05; this deployment sequence continued until T+ 01:04:22, when the final Starlink satellite left the payload bay, lit by one of the three Starlinks equipped with cameras and spotlights. The payload bay door was fully closed by T+ 01:05:04.

Starship has begun deploying its payload of 26 @Starlink V3 satellites. This deployment sequence will take ~30 minutes pic.twitter.com/ycIdAx5Lbe

— SpaceX (@SpaceX) September 28, 2026

At T+ 01:26:46, Dan Huot announced that the teams had decided to take the first contingency landing zone and come back early. This meant Ship 41 would complete just under two orbits and splashdown in the Pacific Ocean just north of Hawaii. While this was a bit disappointing, SpaceX was always going to be very conservative with this flight, because the last thing engineers want is to strand a ship in orbit. 

During the next 45 mins, Starship would coast in orbit partly around the world. During this time, Ship 41 passes over Hurricane Polo, which had recently made landfall on the west coast of Baja California and then Mexico. At points during orbital daylight, the Starlink train that Ship 41 deployed behind the ship itself is seen in several shots during the coast phase and up till the deorbit burn.

Ship 41’s deorbit burn occurred at T+ 2:12:18 just over South Africa and the Cape of Good Hope. After the deorbit burn, Ship 41 fell slowly toward Earth. Ship 41’s reentry fully began around T+02:47:00; however, the light show and the start of plasma formation began around T+2:40:00 as Ship 41 hit thicker and thicker parts of Earth’s atmosphere.

Starship is reentering the atmosphere pic.twitter.com/fvWq4NwD23

— SpaceX (@SpaceX) September 28, 2026

This reentry is actually the smoothest Starship has handled so far, even though it is the fastest reentry speed of all the other controlled reentries. This is because Ship 41 reentered at a shallower angle compared to the suborbital flights. This means it experienced lower peak heat but for a longer period.

After a beautiful reentry and an uneventful one, Starship completed its landing burn and flip maneuver before splashing down in the Pacific Ocean at T+ 03:08:30, which makes this mission three times longer than any other Starship flight to date.

During the mission, SpaceX also confirmed that all 26 V3 Starlinks contacted the network, ground stations, and even user terminals. Over the next few weeks, those 26 Starlinks will raise their orbits to around 400 km before becoming fully operational.

Splashdown confirmed. Congratulations to the entire SpaceX team on the first orbital flight of Starship! pic.twitter.com/urjmiwnvNl

— SpaceX (@SpaceX) September 28, 2026

Although Ship 41 returned during the first contingency checkpoint shortly after payload deployment, this is a major milestone for SpaceX and the Starship program. Ship 41 got to orbit and deployed an operational payload, and Booster 21 completed its entire mission, which bodes well for a catch with Booster 22. SpaceX still has work to do, mainly losing Raptor engines on ascent, boostback, and landing. Hopefully, Flight 15 will be clean and have no Raptor losses.

Flights 15

Following the successful Flight 14, Flight 15 will be Booster 22 and Ship 42, and both are currently in their respective Mega Bays being fitted with Raptor engines.

Currently, Booster 22 is slated to be ready for static fire within the next two weeks, and Ship 42 could be ready within two to three weeks. Accounting for post-static-fire preparations, possible Flight 14-related modifications, and payload loading, Booster 22 and Ship 42 could be flight-ready by the end of October.

The final hold-up will depend on whether SpaceX decides to repeat Flight 14’s mission profile and try for a 10-hour mission with Ship 42. Currently, the Starship Super Heavy launch license covers only Flight 14 and would need to be modified for Flight 15, but the modification process will be quicker if SpaceX opts to fly the same mission.

Pad 2 Servicing Structure Being Installed

After three flights, the now Orbital Launch Mount looks in great shape, and SpaceX is using the new servicing structure to refurbish and service the hold-down arms and clamps, rather than using a scaffolding floor.

It’ll be interesting when Flight 15 launches, because Flight 16 could be from LC-39A. Because as heard from people at Kennedy Space Center, LC-39A has all systems activated and is just waiting for vehicles and its roof to be installed.

Featured Image: Ship 41 and Booster 21 Liftoff for Flight 14 (Credit: Max Evans for NSF)

The post Starship makes orbit, Flight 15 preps in full swing appeared first on NASASpaceFlight.com.

item.title: Launch Preview: Crew-13 to head to ISS, Falcon Heavy mission for the NRO
item.dc:creator: Eleanor Day
item.description:
Four orbital launches are expected this week, all by SpaceX’s Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy…

The post Launch Preview: Crew-13 to head to ISS, Falcon Heavy mission for the NRO appeared first on NASASpaceFlight.com.
item.content:encoded:
Four orbital launches are expected this week, all by SpaceX’s Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy vehicles. From Florida, Crew-13 will launch to the International Space Station while Falcon Heavy will launch a payload for the National Reconnaissance Office from Launch Complex 39A. At Vandenberg, two Falcon 9s are scheduled to launch payloads for the Transporter-18 rideshare mission and the Tranche 1 Transport Layer A constellation. Notably, every mission this week will feature a return-to-launch-site landing.

Falcon 9 | Crew-13

NASA and SpaceX’s Crew-13 mission to the International Space Station (ISS) is expected to launch from Space Launch Complex 40 (SLC-40) at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida on Thursday, Oct. 1. As with most missions to the ISS, Crew-13 requires an instantaneous launch window, currently scheduled for 11:10 AM EDT (15:10 UTC). Falcon 9 will launch on a northeasterly trajectory into an orbit inclined by 51.63 degrees to match the ISS’s orbital plane.

Falcon 9 first-stage booster B1101 will support this mission, flying for the third time and being recovered at Landing Zone 40 (LZ-40) using its return-to-launch-site (RTLS) capabilities. Crew Dragon Grace (C213) will be on its second flight, having previously flown the Axiom-4 mission to the ISS.

Grace is scheduled to deliver four astronauts to the Station, with the vehicle docking to the Harmony forward port at 8:00 PM EDT on Oct. 1. NASA astronaut and commander Jessica Watkins will be on her second spaceflight, with NASA astronaut and pilot Luke Delaney flying on his first mission. Mission Specialists Joshua Kutryk from the Canadian Space Agency (CSA) and Sergey Teteryatnikov (Roscosmos) are also first-time flyers.

Crew-13 will join Expedition 75 aboard the ISS and will depart in March 2027 after approximately six months at the Station. This mission will mark Falcon 9’s 109th mission of 2026 and 692nd overall.

Falcon 9 | Transporter-18

The second Falcon 9 mission of the week is expected to launch from Space Launch Complex 4E (SLC-4E) at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California. Falcon 9 will launch during a one-hour launch window beginning at 11:18 AM PDT (18:18 UTC) on a southerly trajectory to deliver 130 rideshare payloads to a Sun-synchronous orbit (SSO).

Booster B1082 will be recovered at Landing Zone 4 (LZ-4) via an RTLS trajectory. The booster will be flying on its 25th mission, previously supporting the USSF-62, NROL-145, OneWeb Launch 20, and 21 Starlink missions.

One of the 130 rideshare payloads is Terra Nova, a pathfinder satellite developed by NordSpace. The self-funded, dual-use satellite was built to demonstrate key low-Earth operations, including Earth observation, situational awareness, and Rendezvous, Proximity Operations, and Docking (RPOD). The payload is being manifested by Exolaunch, which will be on its 50th rideshare mission across multiple vehicles.

This mission will mark the 110th Falcon 9 mission of 2026 and 693rd overall.

Falcon Heavy | NROL-97

Off the heels of the launch of the Roman Space Telescope in late August, Falcon Heavy is set to return with a launch from Launch Complex 39A (LC-39A) at the Kennedy Space Center in Florida on Thursday, Oct. 1. The vehicle will launch during a 59-minute launch window beginning at 11:53 PM EDT, on a northeasterly trajectory to deliver the classified NROL-97 payload to a high-energy orbit for the National Reconnaissance Office (NRO).

Falcon Heavy’s outer two boosters, B1072 and B1104, will land at Landing Zones 2 (LZ-2) and 1 (LZ-1), respectively. B1072 will be on its fourth flight, having previously supported the launches of the Roman Space Telescope, GOES-U, and ViaSat-3 F3 missions. B1104 will be on its second mission, with the launch of Roman serving as its first mission. The center booster, B1106, will be on its first flight and will be expended.

Falcon Heavy is a super-heavy-lift, partially reusable vehicle that uses three Falcon boosters as its first stage. Each of the vehicle’s boosters uses nine Merlin 1D sea-level-optimized engines, fueled by kerosene (RP-1) and liquid oxygen (LOX). The second stage uses a single Merlin 1D vacuum-optimized engine, which also uses the same propellants. Falcon Heavy has a total liftoff thrust of 22,819 kilonewtons (kN) and can deliver up to 63,000 kg to low-Earth orbit (LEO).

The mission will be Falcon Heavy’s third mission of 2026, and 13th overall.

Falcon 9 | Tranche 1 Transport Layer A

The final mission of the week is expected to launch from SLC-4E at Vandenberg on Monday, Oct. 5. Falcon 9 will launch on a southerly trajectory to a polar orbit during a 65-minute launch window beginning at 1:06 AM PDT (08:06 UTC). The vehicle will deliver 21 payloads for the Tranche 1 Transport Layer A constellation for the United States Space Force Space Development Agency (SDA).

The first-stage booster, which is currently unknown, will perform an RTLS landing at LZ-4. The mission will be the 727th overall mission for SpaceX and the company’s 117th mission of 2026. Furthermore, this mission will serve as the 237th orbital launch attempt worldwide in 2026.

(Lead Image: Falcon 9 launch and landing streak. Credit: Julia Bergeron for NSF)

The post Launch Preview: Crew-13 to head to ISS, Falcon Heavy mission for the NRO appeared first on NASASpaceFlight.com.

item.title: NASA, Boeing outline Starliner’s return path to ISS crew rotations
item.dc:creator: Chris Bergin
item.description:
NASA and Boeing have laid out a revised path for Starliner that puts an uncrewed…

The post NASA, Boeing outline Starliner’s return path to ISS crew rotations appeared first on NASASpaceFlight.com.
item.content:encoded:
NASA and Boeing have laid out a revised path for Starliner that puts an uncrewed engineering flight first, a crewed return in 2028, extra station missions on the books, and a new launcher in the certification pipeline.

Speaking Monday, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman framed the update as part of a broader push to keep more than one U.S. crew transportation option available as demand grows across low Earth orbit.

“We are living through the most exciting era of space exploration since Apollo,” Isaacman said. “NASA has been committed to having multiple crew transportation options since the beginning of the Commercial Crew Program.

“We have worked closely with Boeing to address the issues identified on previous Starliner flights, and we intend to see this vehicle return to flight in support of the International Space Station and future commercial destinations.”

The agency intends to exercise options for a fifth and sixth flight to and from the station using Starliner. In parallel, NASA will work with Boeing and United Launch Alliance to certify ULA’s Vulcan rocket for crew transportation after Atlas V’s remaining flights are used.
Atlas V has been Starliner’s only ride to date, but with production ending, a certified Vulcan is required if the spacecraft is to have a long-term future.

Uncrewed first, crew in 2028

Isaacman said the next mission will not carry astronauts, flying on an uncrewed mission to the ISS to put the vehicle through its paces to ensure corrective action has been successful.

“We are starting with an uncrewed Starliner-1 mission to the International Space Station to validate the improvements made to the spacecraft and gather the flight data we need,” he said.

“From there, we will use what we learn, continue implementing the corrective actions identified by our Program Investigation Team, and complete the testing and certification required for crewed flight. Our current plan is to return astronauts on Starliner-2 by 2028.”

Starliner-1 is targeted no earlier than December 2026, with January 2027 also in the window. NASA describes it as an engineering evaluation flight: verify improved thermal environments on the service module, collect qualification data, and identify residual risk before anyone flies again.
Dana Weigel, manager of NASA’s Low Earth Orbit Program, said the uncrewed mission is the critical step toward full system certification.

“With the safety of our space station crew and the public as our highest priority, we will test Starliner’s propulsion system through targeted demonstration objectives and disciplined operational controls. These steps are essential to validating Starliner’s thermal performance, which is a key element for the certification.”

NASA astronaut Woody Hoburg has been assigned to command the first crewed return, Starliner-2.

What the investigation found

In February, NASA released the Program Investigation Team findings from the 2024 Crew Flight Test, which ended with an uncrewed return after service module reaction control thrusters operated outside their engineering qualification and the vehicle lost control authority during approach. The team issued 61 recommendations.
Ground testing and analysis showed the thruster problems were not a single failure. They came from a combination of the thermal environment around the service module “doghouses” and design features of the thruster valves themselves. Boeing has already made thermal modifications that NASA will evaluate on Starliner-1.

After that flight, NASA and Boeing will implement an additional thruster valve design change aimed at poppet seal extrusion and its effect on thruster performance. Boeing will also install new crew module thrusters, new batteries, and make minor parachute system modifications before crewed certification.

Poppet problem recalls STS-126 incident

Poppet valves are not new to human spaceflight, and neither is trouble with their seals.

Starliner’s service module RCS valves use a poppet with a Teflon seal. Heating, soak-back, and the oxidizer environment can cause that seal to swell and extrude, restricting nitrogen tetroxide flow into the thruster.

White Sands testing after CFT reproduced the degraded performance and found the extruded Teflon poppet as a contributor. The planned valve modification is intended to stop that extrusion from becoming a flight constraint again.

The Shuttle program spent years wrestling with a different but related problem on its Main Propulsion System Flow Control Valves.

United Space Alliance engineer works on Shuttle MPS FCV system – via L2

After a liberation event on STS-126 (Endeavour), managers delayed STS-119 (Discovery) until they had flight rationale for three “cherry-picked” FCVs that had flown without issue. Post-flight inspection of those valves on Discovery showed no cracks, the precursor to liberation, and that result helped clear STS-125 (Atlantis).

Shuttle also dealt with PTFE pilot-seal extrusion on Orbiter primary RCS thruster fuel valves, a known failure mode that produced restricted flow and dozens of ground and on-orbit valve issues over the program’s life.

The systems are not the same, however. Starliner’s doghouse thermal environment, pulse trains, and oxidizer-side poppet geometry are specific to this vehicle.

The historical parallel is simply that poppets and softgoods have a long record of being unforgiving when temperature, pressure, and propellant chemistry line up the wrong way.

Flight data, inspection, and a hardware change were how Shuttle closed those issues. NASA and Boeing are now applying the same sequence to Starliner.

Certification path

Starliner-1 is meant to “close the thermal chapter” in flight. The valve redesign, new crew module thrusters, batteries, and parachute work follow.

Only then does NASA intend to complete the remaining certification work for crewed flight in 2028, with additional missions already optioned and Vulcan in the certification queue so the spacecraft is not stranded when Atlas V is gone.

A ULA Vulcan (USSF-87) sits next to a SpaceX Crew Dragon (Crew-12), via Tyler Gray for NSF.

Isaacman cast the extra missions and the new rocket as part of keeping U.S. crew access intact through the end of station operations and the handoff to commercial destinations.

The work, he and Weigel both emphasized, is still gated by propulsion performance and the high standards required for human spaceflight.

Featured Image: NASA.

The post NASA, Boeing outline Starliner’s return path to ISS crew rotations appeared first on NASASpaceFlight.com.

item.title: Ship 41 Makes it to Orbit, Booster 21 Nearly Perfect
item.dc:creator: Ryan Weber
item.description:
After more than a decade of development in many forms, SpaceX’s Starship has finally reached…

The post Ship 41 Makes it to Orbit, Booster 21 Nearly Perfect appeared first on NASASpaceFlight.com.
item.content:encoded:
After more than a decade of development in many forms, SpaceX’s Starship has finally reached orbit. Ship 41 lifted off at 7:48:59 am CDT from Pad 2 in Starbase, TX, and completed a fully successful mission. While it did not reach the distance and coast for nearly eight hours, SpaceX has completed a very important milestone for the program.

Flight 14

After a seamless countdown and tank farm activation for Starship Flight 14, SpaceX pushed the launch 31 minutes into the window to allow for better lighting at the splashdown locations. SpaceX then pushed another 2 mins or so for a T-0 of 7:48:59 CDT; then at exactly 7:48:59 CDT, Booster 21 and Ship 41 lifted off from Pad 2 at Starbase, TX. Booster 21 lifted off with all 33 engines running, but lost a single center Raptor engine during ascent.

Booster 21 then performed its boost-back burn with only 31 engines on and completed it for the full duration. Then, after a perfect glide back, the booster ignited 11 of 13 engines for the landing burn and splashed down on target in the Gulf. The booster was then intentionally destroyed with the Flight Termination System. Booster 21’s flight was a complete success despite losing some engines in all phases of flight; however, with the success it did have, Booster 22 is set to be the first Block 3 booster to be caught on Flight 15.

Ship 41 completed hot staging with all six engines running before losing a Raptor Vacuum engine partway during ascent. Ship 41 still made it to Second Stage Engine Cutoff, then SpaceX performed health checks to decide whether to attempt orbit. Initially, SpaceX had said no-go for orbit, but mission control talked it over and repolled go for orbit.

Starship performs its orbital insertion burn and enters orbit of Earth for the first time pic.twitter.com/LodrSTnEnl

— SpaceX (@SpaceX) September 28, 2026

Then, at T+25:20, Ship 41 completed its orbital insertion burn, placing the ship into a 262 by 277 km orbit at 32 degrees. Ship 41 then deployed all 26 Starlink V3 satellites into orbit. Once deployed, all 26 Starlinks were fully activated and began connecting with other Starlinks, ground stations, and even user terminals.

After Starlink deployment, SpaceX decided not to perform the full coast phase of this flight and instead reenter at the first contingency landing zone north of Hawaii. This is SpaceX being very conservative and not wanting to leave a ship in orbit, so the engineers and launch controllers opted to bring the ship back early. Ship 41 then completed a successful deorbit burn at T+ 2:12:18, which marks yet another big milestone for Starship.

Ship 41 then reentered Earth’s atmosphere and splashed down at T+ 3:08:30. While SpaceX didn’t get all the data from the long coast phase, they made it to orbit. Starship is now an operational orbital rocket, capable of delivering payloads.

Splashdown confirmed. Congratulations to the entire SpaceX team on the first orbital flight of Starship! pic.twitter.com/urjmiwnvNl

— SpaceX (@SpaceX) September 28, 2026

Flight 12 and 13 Recap

See Also

  • SpaceX Starship Program
  • L2 SpaceX Section
  • NSF Store
  • Click here to Join L2

The past two Starship flights have gone pretty well for the ship, but not as well for the booster. Flight 12 was the first-ever Block 3 Starship stack to fly, and during the flight, Booster 19 had boost-back issues and was lost during its landing burn attempt.

Ship 39 lost a Raptor Vacuum engine during ascent, but still completed its ascent burn and deployed its payload. Ship 39 then reentered and made an on-target splashdown in the Indian Ocean.

Flight 13 went better than Flight 12, with Booster 20 completing a perfect ascent and actually starting all engines for the boost-back burn; however, due to ice ingestion issues, the burn was cut short, and Booster 20 ended up farther offshore than was intended.

Then, during the landing burn, Booster 20 failed to ignite all engines before slamming into the Gulf and exploding.

Booster 20 Raptor Engines at Liftoff

Ship 40 then completed a perfect ascent burn and then deployed all 20 Starlink V3 satellites, which deployed their solar arrays for testing before burning up behind the ship. Ship 40 then completed a perfect reentry before splashing down intact in the Indian Ocean, which surprised SpaceX.

After over a month at sea and engineers removing tiles and other components for study, Ship 40 was loaded onto the ship Forte and is currently in the Atlantic Ocean, set to return on No Earlier Than (NET) Oct. 8.

Why now for an Orbital Attempt?

The last 13 test flights have been suborbital missions to improve the ship and booster over time without risking accidentally leaving a 52-meter-long, nine-meter-wide, 160-metric-ton vehicle in orbit with no control.

With that in mind, SpaceX chose to use suborbital missions to ensure that no matter if teams lost control of the ship, which did happen a few times, the ship would reenter the atmosphere no matter what.

This suborbital track let SpaceX test a full stack: liftoff, stage separation, boost-back and landing burns for the booster, and near-full ascent burns for the ship. In later missions with 40 minutes of coast-phase time, SpaceX engineers tested payload deployment with dummy V3s and eventually full V3 Starlink satellites, as well as in-space Raptor engine relights that simulated a deorbit burn.

Booster 21 and Ship 41 Stacked

Finally, with the ships just shy of orbital velocity, SpaceX gathered strong heat-shield data during the controlled reentries. This helped inform changes like adding ablative material under the tiles, starting with Ship 30, or eliminating heat shield seams to better seal gaps between the tiles. 

With this information, SpaceX made significant changes to the launch pad, booster, and ship over time. This resulted in a newly designed launch pad, which is now being constructed at three launch pads at Cape Canaveral; Pad 1 was demolished and is being retrofitted, and at least 10 are planned at Starbase, LA.

This information also led to a clean-sheet design for the Block 3 booster with an integrated hotstage ring and important internal upgrades, as well as an upgraded ship design for longer-duration missions in orbit and eventually to return the ship to the launch site.

With all of these upgraded systems and two flights using the newer booster and ship, SpaceX is ready to attempt an orbital mission, deploy 26 Starlink V3 satellites, and then perform a deorbit burn to splashdown in the South Pacific Ocean.

Booster 21 Static Fire

Launch Windows, Launch License Changes

The launch date for Flight 14/Starlink Group 31-1 is set for Sept. 28 at 7:15 am CDT with a 75-minute launch window. Backup days run from Sept. 29 to Oct. 4, with current Notices to Airmen and Notices to Mariners. The road closures for this launch are a bit shorter than in the past. For Flight 14, SpaceX will close the beach and road starting at 4 am CDT and reopen them at 10 am CDT.

This is much shorter than past launches were; SpaceX would keep the road closed for nearly 10 to 12 hours. It shows the confidence and efficiency of SpaceX’s new tank farm and range operations.

To perform this mission, SpaceX had to obtain an updated launch license from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). SpaceX not only received a revised license, but also a reentry license for Starship. The original launch license for Starship included launch and reentry under the same definition section; now it’s split into two sections within the same license.

The license is No. VOL 23-129 Rev 9.0 Order A-1 for launch and Order A-2 for reentry, which places both under the same license. This differs from older FAA licensing and is part of the new Part 450 of the Federal Aviation Regulations. Order A-1 now covers initial liftoff and suborbital flight, should SpaceX not go into orbit.

Order A-2 now gives Starship permission to reenter from orbit and splashdown in the Pacific Ocean, as stated in the application, covering the splashdown zone north of Hawaii and the intended zone off the coast of Chile in the South Pacific Ocean. This Order only authorizes Starship-Super Heavy Flight 14, so SpaceX will need another modification for Flight 15 and beyond. Eventually, the FAA will add LC-39A to this launch license.

Starship Flight 14 has its launch license! All go for Monday!https://t.co/lRC3NXhsMZ pic.twitter.com/AMndKjmq69

— NSF – NASASpaceflight.com (@NASASpaceflight) September 26, 2026

Mission Objectives, Trajectory, and Launch Timeline

This flight uses Booster 21 and Ship 41; compared to Booster 20 and Ship 40, only a few changes are worth noting. Ship 41’s heat shield has the newer extended ablative, which moves the heat shield back toward the leeward side, like Ship 30’s, and extends it as far as the early ships. Booster 21 has had the aerocovers above the outer 20 Raptor engines removed; SpaceX appears to have decided they aren’t needed going forward.

Before listing the important mission objectives for Ship 41, it is also an important mission for Booster 21. Because Booster 19 and Booster 20 had issues during the past two flights, SpaceX will not attempt to catch Booster 21; instead, engineers will aim for the booster to complete a mission like Booster 11. This would include a full ascent, boost-back, and landing burn on target in the Gulf. SpaceX needs Booster 21 to succeed because teams want to move into booster reuses as soon as possible.

 

Deployment of 20 @Starlink V3 satellites complete. Today's test will provide critical data as we prepare to expand our Starlink constellation pic.twitter.com/jWKLwXGlsk

— SpaceX (@SpaceX) July 24, 2026

The mission objectives, trajectory, and timeline for this launch differ from the past 13 Starship flights. The primary mission objective for this flight is to reach orbit, deploy 26 Starlink V3 satellites into a 32-degree inclination orbit, then deorbit over the South Pacific Ocean and splashdown after about an eight-hour coast phase following payload deployment.

A splashdown after an eight-hour coast phase isn’t the only way this mission can end; SpaceX will be very conservative because, as noted above, teams don’t want to leave a ship stranded in orbit.

The mission trajectory starts similarly to the last two launches, launching from Starbase, TX, and threading the needle between Jamaica and Cuba before passing through the Leeward Islands and entering a 32-degree inclination suborbital trajectory. Inclination is the angle of an orbit that is relative to Earth’s equatorial plane. After Starship Engine Cutoff (SECO) at about T+ 8:11, Ship 41 will be in a suborbital trajectory to splashdown in the Indian Ocean.

Starship Flight 14 Aborts and Coast Phases (Credit: SpaceX)

This ensures that if any issues arise during ascent or during the checkout phase after SECO, SpaceX can abort the attempt to reach orbit and splashdown in the Indian Ocean. Assuming Ship 41 passes all checks and SpaceX is comfortable going to orbit, the teams will command the ship to initiate the orbital insertion and circulation burn at about T+ 25:19, which will last about 18 seconds. This burn should bring Ship 41 into an approximately 275 km by 275 km orbit around Earth.

Following that burn, Ship 41 will then deploy all 26 Starlink V3 satellites from about T+ 34:09 to about T+ 1:04:41. Once payload deployment is completed, SpaceX will perform another health check on all ship systems; this is to determine if Ship 41 is good to complete at least six hours of the eight-hour coast phase. If SpaceX engineers see something they don’t like, they will command Ship 41 to reenter just north of Hawaii in the Central Pacific Ocean just before completing two full orbits.

Assuming Ship 41 passes those health checks, it will coast for about six hours while engineers continue to monitor systems for any issues that may arise. Then, after a few orbits, SpaceX will run another health check about two hours before the end of the mission to determine whether Ship 41 can continue to the end or must return a bit earlier. If Ship 41 passes all health checks at each milestone, the deorbit burn for the final splashdown zone is set to commence at approximately T+ 8:52:37 and will last about 10 seconds.

Starship in space on Flight 13 pic.twitter.com/rAxl8BqHsK

— SpaceX (@SpaceX) July 28, 2026

This will then bring Ship 41 on a trajectory to land just off the coast of Chile in the South Pacific Ocean. Reentry is set to start at around T+ 9:29:02 and will continue until Starship initiates its landing burn at about T+ 9:50:11. Total mission completion is set at about 9 hours, 50 minutes, and 30 seconds.

It is unknown whether SpaceX will attempt to recover Ship 41 if it survives the full flight and splashdown, but it may want to collect heat shield samples if possible.

Beyond attempting orbit, SpaceX is also testing two tiles on Ship 41’s aft that it removed from Ship 40 as it floated off the coast of Christmas Island. It is also testing other improvements based on data gathered from Ship 40. These include additional retention mechanisms for tiles that had retention issues during ascent, as well as a curved tile design to reduce heating in gaps between tiles.

Ship 40 tiles on Ship 41’s Aft Skirt

As stated above, Ship 41 will attempt to deploy 26 Starlink V3s into orbit, adding 1 Tbps of capacity to the Starlink network per satellite once operational. These 26 satellites provide 10 times the capacity of a single Falcon 9 launch of Starlink V2 minis.

SpaceX has many objectives for this historic Starship flight, and hopefully Ship 41 can complete the entire planned mission while Booster 21 performs all aspects perfectly so Booster 22 can be caught on the next flight.

Featured Image: Booster 21 and Ship 41 in Flight (Credit: Ceasar G)

The post Ship 41 Makes it to Orbit, Booster 21 Nearly Perfect appeared first on NASASpaceFlight.com.

item.title: Flight 14 approaches as a near-term manifest sketches Starship’s next steps
item.dc:creator: Alejandro Alcantarilla Romera and Chris Bergin
item.description:
With Flight 14 being Starship’s first intended orbital mission, a near-term manifest is already pointing…

The post Flight 14 approaches as a near-term manifest sketches Starship’s next steps appeared first on NASASpaceFlight.com.
item.content:encoded:
With Flight 14 being Starship’s first intended orbital mission, a near-term manifest is already pointing to the next two flights in close succession.

Those dates look optimistic, and they may well slip, but they do confirm SpaceX is lining up a three-flight stretch from Flights 14 through 16: an orbital attempt from Starbase, a possible return to catching, and Starship’s expected East Coast debut.

Booster 21 and Ship 41 rolled out earlier this week after months of pre-launch testing and preparations, then stacked at the pad for a wet dress rehearsal while SpaceX waited on approval.

From the outside, that test appeared to go well. Both stages were fully loaded with propellant, there were no apparent holds at the optional T-minus 60-second hold point, and the count continued to just before engine ignition before the launch mount’s top-deck water deluge started and shut down a few seconds later.

Full Stack WDR

Next step: Launch License!

@NASASpaceflight pic.twitter.com/1vnv36XZ0u

— Jerry Pike (@JerryPikePhoto) September 24, 2026

Ship 41, already loaded with 26 Starlink V3 satellites, was destacked from Booster 21 on Friday but remained at the launch site.

A full stack nearly a week before the planned launch had raised questions about timing, but SpaceX said teams were using the regulatory pause to get an extra rehearsal in.

Earlier Starship versions rarely scrubbed close to launch; with Version 3, the first two flights have each seen a scrub of some kind. The extra pad time also put the launch mount back into use more than two months after the last flight.

Approval could still arrive at any time, including over the weekend, so a Monday launch remains possible even without a license in hand tonight. UPDATE: APPROVAL ARRIVED ON SATURDAY.

The October dates come from presentation slides posted through the CADENA air traffic management system, which flags upcoming events, weather, and other factors that could affect air traffic across North and South America.

As expected, the briefing dwells on the airspace impact of Flight 14 next week and notes other space activity, including Falcon launches, but it also lists additional “upcoming high-profile missions.”

This is super provisional!

Starship Flight 15 – NET October 19
Starship Flight 16 (Starlink 30-1) – KSC 39A – NET October 30.

You can bet those dates will slip, but it shows some of SpaceX's forward planning. pic.twitter.com/aB7KihBsH8

— NSF – NASASpaceflight.com (@NASASpaceflight) September 24, 2026

Those entries put Starship Flight 15 no earlier than Oct. 19 and another Starship launch, Starlink Group 30-1, no earlier than Oct. 30. Flight 15 is understood to be the next Starbase mission after Flight 14 and the flight that could restore catching, possibly of both vehicles.

See Also

  • SpaceX Starship Program
  • L2 SpaceX Section
  • NSF Store
  • Click here to Join L2

Starlink Group 30-1 is expected to be the first Starship launch from Launch Complex 39A in Florida; as with Flight 14, that East Coast mission has been given a Starlink designation, in this case 30-1 rather than 31-1.

The dates should be treated cautiously. SpaceX still needs a clean Flight 14 outcome; the Flight 15 vehicles still require their own engine testing, and some of the slide dates may already be days or weeks old. Extra regulatory approval, including for a possible ship catch on Flight 15, could push the schedule further.

A Florida launch would also require vehicles to be moved east and the pad to be fully activated. SpaceX tested LC-39A’s top-deck deluge system for the first time Thursday night, a sign the pad is getting closer, but it still lacks a license to fly Starship from 39A.

BREAKING NEWS

For the first time, moments ago, SpaceX tested the top deck deluge of the Starship launch mount at historic LC-39A in Florida!

See if they keep testing more tonight by watching the @NASASpaceflight 24/7 livestream, https://t.co/ejPQM0oNEh! pic.twitter.com/Znw3e5dF7T

— MattZ (@wvmattz) September 25, 2026

Those October targets are likely to spread out in the weeks ahead. They only hold if Flight 14 does what Version 3 has not done yet: get through the count, reach orbit, and bring a working ship home through reentry. Until that happens, the manifest is a sketch. Flight 14 remains the key focus to set the stage for the next milestones.

Lead image: SpaceX

Flight 14 coverage plans

NASASpaceflight plans expanded coverage of Flight 14. Launch coverage is set to begin at T-minus 4 hours and continue through payload deployment.

If Starship is approved to remain in orbit, coverage would then shift to an orbital stakeout stream through the vehicle’s nearly eight-hour coast before deorbit and reentry. Dedicated deorbit, entry, and splashdown coverage would begin about 30 minutes before the deorbit burn.

The opening of the current window is 7:15 a.m. local time at Starbase, which could produce a sunrise launch. NASASpaceflight teams are already on site.

item.title: Expedition 75 astronauts continue science work as Crew-13 readies for launch
item.dc:creator: Justin Davenport

The post Expedition 75 astronauts continue science work as Crew-13 readies for launch appeared first on NASASpaceFlight.com.
item.content:encoded:
AS the International Space Station continues to orbit Earth as it has for over a quarter of a century, the Expedition 75 astronauts aboard have been busy performing science and maintenance tasks, and preparing for new arrivals and a crew handover early next month.

Just before the end of August, the Cygnus XL cargo ship S.S. Steven R. Nagel reboosted the Station to prepare for the upcoming Progress MS-35 cargo flight, which at the time was scheduled to fly on Sept. 9. Following on from three spacewalks made from the US segment of the ISS in August, another EVA was carried out on Sept. 1.

Sophie Adenot, as EV1 with red stripes on her space suit, and Jessica Meir, as EV2, conducted US EVA-99, returning to the Station’s Quest airlock module after six hours and 49 minutes outside. The astronauts installed a new retroreflector on the Harmony node module’s forward port to support navigation for visiting vehicles.

Sophie Adenot outside the ISS during EVA-99. (Credit: ESA/NASA)

Adenot and Meir also replaced a high-definition camera on the Station’s truss assembly and swabbed the Station’s exterior for microorganism samples. The astronauts began installing jumper cables for electrical systems and started work on replacing the Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer’s radiator assembly, tasks that will be finished on a future spacewalk.

During the spacewalk, Sophie Adenot experienced mobility issues in her left shoulder, which were traced to a joint heater harness getting caught in the shoulder joint. Meir unzipped the joint, which appeared to solve the issue. Various issues with the aging Shuttle-era suits have delayed Station spacewalks and forced repairs on various suit parts, which can be returned to Earth aboard Cargo Dragon spacecraft for evaluation and maintenance if required.

EVA-99 was the 248th spacewalk overall in support of the ISS, and marked Meir’s seventh and Adenot’s third spacewalk. Jessica Meir is now NASA’s third most experienced female spacewalker, behind only Peggy Whitson and Suni Williams. Two additional spacewalks are planned for Expedition 75 to install iROSA solar arrays on the 3B and 2A power channels, although scheduling of this work has not yet been announced.

Progress MS-35 docking to the Poisk module of the Russian Orbital Segment. (Credit: NASA+)

A week after EVA-99, Progress MS-33 undocked from the Russian segment’s Poisk module to make room for the upcoming Progress MS-35 flight. Loaded with trash, MS-33 burned up on reentry on Sept. 7,  ahead of the planned launch of MS-35 on Sept. 9, although the launch was subsequently delayed by a hydraulic issue with the rocket.

NASA also announced that the upcoming Crew-13 flight to the Station would be delayed due to an oxidizer leak on Crew Dragon Grace. The flight is now set for Oct. 1, and Crew-13 astronauts entered quarantine on Sept. 17. When Crew-13 arrives, astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney of NASA, Canada’s Joshua Kutryk, and Roscosmos’ Sergey Teteryatnikov will relieve their Crew-12 counterparts after a short handover period.

Progress MS-35 launched on Sept. 16, successfully docking with the Poisk module on Sept. 19 at 13:44 UTC. MS-35, also designated Progress 96 or 96P by NASA, delivered roughly 2,600 kg of cargo for the Station and its crew. As of Sept. 24, there are five visiting vehicles at the ISS: Progress MS-34 and MS-35, Soyuz MS-29, Dragon Freedom on the Crew-12 mission, and the NG-24 Cygnus S.S. Steven R. Nagel.

Anil Menon working with a lead-free soldering experiment. (Credit: ESA/Sophie Adenot)

The Expedition 75 crew conducts a daily schedule of science and maintenance tasks. Recent science highlights have included a lead-free soldering experiment in the Harmony module. NASA’s Anil Menon set up a work area in Harmony and soldered components on a circuit board. His work will now be returned to Earth so it can be compared with another circuit board that was soldered on the ground. Soldering components in flight may reduce reliance on resupply flights during future space missions by enabling more repairs to be carried out in-situ.

Other science highlights included a 3D colloidal crystal experiment, observing particles suspended in liquids, with possible space-based manufacturing applications. Sophie Adenot set up the Kubik research incubator and centrifuge for remote operations by scientists on the ground. Many experiments on the ISS are controlled this way.

Adenot has been working extensively with the Advanced Resistive Exercise Device (ARED) in the Tranquility module, recording her workouts using a motion capture system. She is also evaluating the European Enhanced Exploration Exercise Device (E4D) set up in the Columbus science module, including rope-pulling exercises which had never been done in space before.

The waning gibbous Moon over Earth’s horizon seen from the ISS. (Credit: NASA)

Astronauts are required to exercise for at least two hours per day to mitigate the effects of microgravity on the body, such as muscle atrophy and weakening of bones. Cosmonauts Andrey Fedyaev and Anna Kikina have been evaluating a Russian lower-body negative pressure suit. This suit forces blood back toward the lower body and feet, reversing the typical fluid shift toward the head that occurs in microgravity. Future crews may use these suits to assist with adaptation to Earth’s gravity as they prepare to return home at the end of their spaceflights.

While Crew-13 is due to arrive in October and Crew-12 will subsequently return to Earth, Expedition 75 will continue until the spring of 2027 and the planned departure of Soyuz MS-29.

While day-to-day operations continue on the Station, NASA signed a contract modification with SpaceX to fly the upcoming Crew-15, Crew-16, and Crew-17 missions. These missions have readiness dates in 2027 and 2028, as NASA prepares to end Station operations around 2030. NASA is continuing to work with Boeing to resolve outstanding issues with its Starliner spacecraft to support future commercial space station missions.

(Lead image: The International Space Station orbiting over Central Asia. Credit: NASA/Anil Menon)
